bibliography.checked_against: the title page (PDF p. 3) and the Internet Archive record
bibliography.note: Kendall, William Converse, Scientific Assistant, U.S. Bureau of Fisheries; Appendix V to the Report of the U.S. Commissioner of Fisheries for 1917; Bureau of Fisheries Document No. 853; GPO, Washington, 1917; 45 p. The chain pickerel is treated as the "Eastern pickerel (Esox reticulatus)", pp. 24–34

claims.claim: Kendall (1917) found very young Maine pickerel "find their way into the shallowest waters and mouths of brooks entering the lake" (anecdotal)
claims.source_value: a general statement about the species, with no place named and no observation behind it: "The very young, just as in the case of many other fishes, find their way into…"
claims.quote: find their way into the shallowest waters and mouths of brooks entering the lake
claims.conditions: follows a remark that pickerel found far upstream "probably reached those places for self-protection while young fish"; ends "probably from neighboring localities where they were born"
claims.note: drop "Maine" and "found": write "Kendall (1917) wrote that very young pickerel find their way…"

claims.claim: young pickerel find "the shallowest waters and mouths of brooks entering the lake" (Kendall 1917, Maine)
claims.source_value: the same general statement; no place is named
claims.quote: The very young, just as in the case of many other fishes
claims.note: the quoted words are right; "Maine" is not in the source's sentence

claims.claim: young of 51–102 mm at Umbagog Lake held only Entomostraca and insect larvae
claims.quote: ranging from 2 to 4 inches long were found to be feeding exclusively upon Entomostraca
claims.conditions: Umbagog Lake (Maine and New Hampshire); "many young pickerel", number not given; 2–4 in = 51–102 mm (length type not stated)
claims.note: the row's other parts (plankters for a week, fish principal only after 102–152 mm) are Scott & Crossman's; Kendall's own examples are consistent: a < 2.5-in fish with a young sucker, a 3.2-in fish with a sunfish, and six of eight 4.25–6.37-in fish with fish

claims.claim: of eight pickerel of 108–162 mm caught together (place not stated), six held fish, and four of the prey were young pickerel
claims.quote: Of eight examples, from 4.25 to 6.37 inches in length, caught at the same time
claims.conditions: "in the same place", not named; 4.25–6.37 in = 108–162 mm

claims.claim: among Kendall's Maine and New Hampshire stomach records, six of eight young pickerel of 108–162 mm, caught together at an unstated place, held fish, four of those prey smaller pickerel; pickerel prey reached 0.71 of the cannibal's length (project calculation)
claims.quote: a 4.25-inch fish had also a young pickerel 3 inches long
claims.conditions: the 4.25-in cannibal is "of another lot", not one of the eight; other cannibals: 5.37 in with a 3-in pickerel (0.56), 5.87 in with 2.06 in (0.35), 6.37 in with 3 in (0.47), 9½ in with 2.3 in (0.24)
claims.note: 3 / 4.25 = 0.706. The cannibalism records carry no place; only the surrounding diet records are from Maine and Umbagog (Maine–New Hampshire), so "Maine and New Hampshire stomach records" is loose but the sentence itself says the place is unstated

claims.paper: src/config.js:480; src/config.js:498 (EGG3 pike pred 0.1: "~10 % eaten, Kendall")
claims.claim: about 10 % of pickerel eggs are eaten by predators over the egg stage
claims.quote: fully 10 per cent of eggs deposited are devoured by other fishes
claims.conditions: a Pennsylvania hatchery superintendent's estimate, relayed by Kendall; "fully" = at least 10 %; the same writer saw storms wash "hundreds of millions" of eggs ashore
claims.note: cite as an estimate relayed by Kendall (a lower bound), not a measurement

claims.claim: a Sebago pickerel < 64 mm held a 13-mm sucker
claims.quote: One less than 2.5 inches long contained a young sucker
claims.conditions: "about one-half an inch in length", partly digested; < 2.5 in = < 64 mm, ½ in = 13 mm
claims.note: the sentence follows the Sebago Lake examples but does not repeat the place, and the next example is from "the brook in which the fish were found"; Sebago is a likely reading, not an explicit one

notes: Only the place attached to the shallow-water/brook-mouth remark needs changing (no place in the source). Other values in the account the rewrite might use: Maine stomach records of adult pickerel with hornpouts (Sebois River, Wissatoquoik Deadwater) and Umbagog pickerel 'usually' with small suckers (p. 27); pickerel breed in 3–10 ft of water in shallow coves, inlet mouths and overflowed areas (p. 28); chubs (Semotilus bullaris) seen gorged with pickerel 2–3 in long (pp. 33–34); a 1:14 male:female ratio from the Massachusetts commissioners (p. 29).
